'''Suzanne A. Blum''' is an American professor of chemistry at the [[University of California, Irvine]]. Blum works on mechanistic chemistry, most recently focusing on borylation reactions and the development of single-molecule and single-particle fluorescence microscopy to study organic chemistry and catalysis. She received the [[American Chemical Society]]'s [[Arthur C. Cope Scholar Award]] in 2023.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=ACS 2023 National Award winners |url=https://cen.acs.org/people/awards/ACS-2023-National-Award-winners/100/i32 |access-date=2022-10-31 |website=cen.acs.org}}</ref>

== Education ==
Blum studied chemistry as an undergraduate at the [[University of Michigan]]. She participated in multiple teaching and research projects, winning outstanding [[American Chemical Society]] student chapter, the UM Alumni Leadership award, and a [[National Science Foundation]] fellowship to attend graduate school at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where she earned a PhD working with [[Robert G. Bergman]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://lsa.umich.edu/content/dam/chem-assets/chem-docs/00newsletter.pdf|title=University of Michigan Chemistry Newsletter|last=Marino|first=J.P.|date=2000|access-date=18 October 2018}}</ref> Blum published multiple first-author papers and received teaching awards throughout her tenure at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. She completed a postdoctoral fellowship at [[Harvard Medical School]] in 2006.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Professor Blum |url=https://blumgroupuci.squarespace.com/professor-blum |access-date=2022-08-27 |website=University of California, Irvine |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Research ==
Prof. Blum began her independent research career in 2006 at the [[University of California, Irvine]] (UCI). Blum’s research focuses on the development and mechanistic study of reactions in organic, organometallic, catalytic, and materials chemistry, and on monitoring reaction intermediates by a combination of traditional spectroscopy and fluorescence microscopy methods. While many of her initial independent research publications were based on activated complexes of gold or palladium catalysts,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hirner |first1=Joshua J. |last2=Shi |first2=Yili |last3=Blum |first3=Suzanne A. |date=2011 |title=Organogold Reactivity with Palladium, Nickel, and Rhodium: Transmetalation, Cross-Coupling, and Dual Catalysis |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ar200055y |journal=Accounts of Chemical Research |language=en |volume=44 |issue=8 |pages=603–613 |doi=10.1021/ar200055y |pmid=21644576 |issn=0001-4842|url-access=subscription }}</ref> she has more recently focused on borylation reactions to make advanced oxygen-, nitrogen-, or sulfur-containing heterocycles,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Issaian |first1=Adena |last2=Tu |first2=Kim N. |last3=Blum |first3=Suzanne A. |date=2017 |title=Boron–Heteroatom Addition Reactions via Borylative Heterocyclization: Oxyboration, Aminoboration, and Thioboration |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.accounts.7b00365 |journal=Accounts of Chemical Research |language=en |volume=50 |issue=10 |pages=2598–2609 |doi=10.1021/acs.accounts.7b00365 |pmid=28933550 |issn=0001-4842|url-access=subscription }}</ref> amenable to pharmaceutical and agricultural derivation. Since starting her independent career, Blum developed single-molecule and single-particle techniques, often borrowed from biological or physical contexts, to study chemical processes, including to observe intermediates in "classical" reactions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cordes |first1=Thorben |last2=Blum |first2=Suzanne A. |date=2013 |title=Opportunities and challenges in single-molecule and single-particle fluorescence microscopy for mechanistic studies of chemical reactions |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nchem.1800 |journal=Nature Chemistry |language=en |volume=5 |issue=12 |pages=993–999 |doi=10.1038/nchem.1800 |pmid=24256861 |bibcode=2013NatCh...5..993C |issn=1755-4349|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hanada |first1=Erin M. |last2=Tagawa |first2=Tristen Kazumasa Soriano |last3=Kawada |first3=Masamu |last4=Blum |first4=Suzanne A. |date=2022-07-13 |title=Reactivity Differences of Rieke Zinc Arise Primarily from Salts in the Supernatant, Not in the Solids |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |language=en |volume=144 |issue=27 |pages=12081–12091 |doi=10.1021/jacs.2c02471 |pmid=35767838 |s2cid=250146552 |issn=0002-7863|pmc=9970556 |bibcode=2022JAChS.14412081H }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Eivgi |first1=Or |last2=Blum |first2=Suzanne A. |date=2022 |title=Real-Time Polymer Viscosity–Catalytic Activity Relationships on the Microscale |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/jacs.2c03711 |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |language=en |volume=144 |issue=30 |pages=13574–13585 |doi=10.1021/jacs.2c03711 |pmid=35866383 |bibcode=2022JAChS.14413574E |s2cid=250954171 |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Blum was elected Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) in 2017 for distinguished contributions to molecular chemistry, particularly for the development of synthetic methods and of fluorescence microscopy tools to study chemical processes.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-11-20 |title=10 faculty honored as AAAS fellows |url=https://provost.uci.edu/2017/11/20/10-faculty-honored-aaas-fellows/ |access-date=2022-08-27
